nature-eecon-028.title: Life cycle thinking: from raw material to rubbish
nature-eecon-028.text:
A greener factory is no gain if it makes the product dirtier to use. Life cycle thinking guards against that. It looks at a product's environmental impacts at every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal, and tries to reduce them. A core aim is to avoid burden shifting, where an improvement at one stage causes harm at another, adding to {{ref:nature-found-023}}.

Companies use it to design greener products, consumers to choose products, and governments to write regulations. Its tools include life-cycle assessment, life cycle management, {{ref:nature-eecon-029}}, {{ref:nature-gov-066}}, product-service systems and {{ref:nature-eecon-030}}. Life-cycle assessment follows impacts from raw material extraction through manufacture, distribution, use, repair, disposal and recycling. The EU Waste Framework Directive brought this thinking into waste policy.

nature-eecon-027.title: Eco-efficiency: more value, less damage
nature-eecon-027.text:
In 1992 the World Business Council for Sustainable Development coined the term eco-efficiency in its publication 'Changing Course', and the 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}} endorsed it. It means providing {{ref:nature-econ-122}} that meet human needs while steadily cutting their environmental impact and resource use over their whole life cycle. Put simply: more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution.

It is measured as a ratio, such as {{ref:nature-econ-483}} produced per unit of CO2 emitted. Alongside consistency and eco-sufficiency, it is one of the three basic sustainability strategies. It relies on technological innovation, business, markets and an acceptance of growth.

That reliance draws criticism. Huesemann and Huesemann showed with historical evidence that efficiency gains have not reduced overall resource use and pollution. Critics argue efficiency alone is not enough, though the point remains debated.

nature-eecon-034.title: Product stewardship: everyone shares the responsibility
nature-eecon-034.text:
Australia's TV and computer scheme has recycled about 230,000 tonnes of e-waste under the country's Product Stewardship Act 2011. That act created voluntary, co-regulatory and mandatory schemes. Under product stewardship, everyone who makes, sells, buys, uses or disposes of a product shares responsibility for its impacts. Those are its environmental and health effects over its whole life, the focus of {{ref:nature-eecon-028}}.

For manufacturers, it includes planning, and if necessary paying, for recycling or disposal at end of life. Products can be redesigned to use fewer harmful substances and to be more durable, reusable and recyclable. It differs from extended producer responsibility, which puts the burden on manufacturers alone. This approach spreads it to retailers, consumers and recyclers too.

nature-eecon-035.title: Container deposits: a refund for every bottle
nature-eecon-035.text: A container deposit scheme adds a refundable fee to a bottle or container, which the buyer gets back on returning it. The refund is an {{ref:nature-econ-089}} to bring containers back. Anyone who finds and returns a bottle can claim it, so collecting them is a means of survival for some homeless people in US cities. Unclaimed fees can pay for landfill or litter control. The same idea applies to paint and tyres, where buyers pay up front for disposing of the toxic waste they become.

nature-eecon-017.title: Industrial symbiosis: one firm's waste, another's input
nature-eecon-017.text:
At Kalundborg in Denmark, a power station's gypsum by-product becomes raw material for a plasterboard maker. That is industrial symbiosis, a part of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}} in which separate firms exchange materials, energy, water and by-products. Such networks use material and energy better than any single process could alone.

Collaboration and nearness are seen as the keys, though being close is neither necessary nor sufficient. Kalundborg's web of exchanges evolved spontaneously over a long time; designing one from above in a short time is hard. Information is a barrier too: by-products are usually treated as waste and listed on no exchange. Keeping resources in use longer eases demands on Earth's resources, a stepping-stone toward a {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}.

nature-eecon-018.title: Eco-industrial parks: neighbors that share
nature-eecon-018.text: An eco-industrial park is a group of businesses on shared land that work together on environmental and resource issues. The goal is better environmental, economic and social performance for all of them. Firms in such parks physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, a form of {{ref:nature-eecon-017}}. They may share waste treatment, pass by-products between plants, and reuse one plant's processed water in another.

nature-eecon-056.title: Food waste valorization: from scraps to feed
nature-eecon-056.text: About 30% of the food livestock eat comes from food waste or from crops grown and processed in the supply chain. Food waste valorization turns food waste into food or feed products, or extracts food or feed ingredients from it. It is a branch of {{ref:nature-eecon-055}}. Landfilled food waste releases methane and other harmful compounds. Processed instead, it can yield biofertilizers, {{ref:nature-eecon-012}}, biofuels, chemicals and nutraceuticals, and it can even be turned into insect protein.

nature-eecon-012.title: Bioplastics: plastic from living sources
nature-eecon-012.text: Biodegradable plastic has been made from chicken feathers, which are 90% keratin and over 6 million tons of waste a year in the EU and US. Bioplastics are a family of plastics made from biological rather than fossil sources, with different properties and uses. Some are made from sugar by genetically modified microbes. They are one of the material products of the {{ref:nature-eecon-009}}.

nature-eecon-011.title: Cascading use of biomass: highest value first
nature-eecon-011.text: Cascading use processes biomass in an ordered pattern so that it yields the highest-value products before lower-value ones. The order runs from fine chemicals and medicines, through chemicals, bioplastics and transport fuels, down to electricity and heat. Those last need the most biomass for the least value. Finding the best pattern for a given biomass is called biorefining, a core skill of the {{ref:nature-eecon-009}}.

nature-eecon-023.title: Source reduction: stopping waste before it starts
nature-eecon-023.text: The surest way to deal with waste is to never make it. Source reduction cuts hazardous and other waste before it arises, by changing how things are produced, the top step of the {{ref:nature-eecon-022}}. It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product recipes, and is sometimes called pollution prevention. A more controversial form, toxics use reduction, targets the use of toxic chemicals early in production. Chemical manufacturers have opposed it.

nature-eecon-037.title: Servitization: selling the service, not the thing
nature-eecon-037.text: Servitization meets customer needs by selling a product's function or output, or a product-service package, rather than the product itself. It turns a one-time sale into a long-term service relationship, such as a maintenance-free service contract. It can also give access to people who cannot afford to buy outright, as with car-pooling, car-sharing or rent-to-own. Alongside optimizing and digitizing, servitizing is one of three main ways to dematerialize a product, and the heart of a {{ref:nature-eecon-036}}.

nature-eecon-051.title: Sustainable materials management: the whole life of stuff
nature-eecon-051.text: During the 20th century, global raw material use rose about twice as fast as population. Each 1 percent rise in GDP has raised raw material use by 0.4 percent. Sustainable materials management responds with a systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle. Unlike waste management, which deals only with end-of-life waste, it holds every industry and consumer along the way responsible. The OECD and the US EPA have adopted it; the OECD issued a policy brief on it in 2012.

nature-eecon-052.title: The linear economy: take, make, waste
nature-eecon-052.text: The conventional economy runs in a straight line: resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away. This linear 'take-make-waste' economy uses up finite reserves of {{ref:nature-res-248}} to make short-lived products that end in landfills or incinerators. It puts great pressure on the environment through extraction, energy-hungry production and huge amounts of waste. The circular economy and {{ref:nature-eecon-024}} are both defined against it.

nature-eecon-030.title: Integrated product policy: acting where it counts
nature-eecon-030.text: Integrated product policy is a form of {{ref:nature-pol-018}} that reduces product-related environmental damage by acting at whichever life-cycle stage works best. Rather than rely on one measure, it combines economic instruments, bans on substances, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines. The European Commission issued a green paper, a discussion document, on it on 7 February 2001.

nature-eecon-029.title: Life cycle costing: the full price of owning something
nature-eecon-029.text: Life cycle costing adds up all the costs a product or system incurs over its whole life, to find the cheapest way of providing it. The sticker price is only the start. {{ref:nature-eecon-028}} shows that the environmental cost of owning a product depends on its running costs for energy and consumables. Product-service systems use life cycle costing by lowering the maintenance and storage costs a consumer would otherwise bear.

nature-eecon-024.title: Circular fashion: clothes that come back around
nature-eecon-024.text: A 2017 Ellen MacArthur Foundation report, 'A New Textiles Economy', brought circular fashion into the mainstream. It applies the {{ref:nature-eecon-001}} to clothing, so that fashion products last longer and are reused, recycled or repurposed instead of discarded. It replaces the take-make-use-dispose model with reduce, reuse, recycle and regenerate. Practices include designing clothes for longevity, using sustainable materials, running recycling programs and supporting second-hand markets.

nature-eecon-025.title: Circular procurement: buying for the loop
nature-eecon-025.text: Circular procurement means buying goods and services that follow circular economy principles, favoring reuse, durability and recycling to extend product lives and cut waste. It may mean buying durable or reusable goods, shared-use models, refurbished assets or products with recycled content. It is often seen as part of {{ref:nature-pol-234}} and supports SDG 12's target on sustainable public procurement. Risks include greenwashing. Barriers include high infrastructure costs and a lack of standard definitions.

nature-eecon-054.title: Urban mining: digging gold out of old gadgets
nature-eecon-054.text: A 2010 Japanese government study estimated that 6,800 tonnes of gold could be recovered from used electronics in Japan. Urban mining recovers rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment. Its main aim is winning back materials, whereas landfill mining aims to fix problems at the disposal site. In developing countries e-waste is often recycled informally, even inside homes, without proper equipment. Shifting from primary production to urban mining needs detailed accounts of materials in use and in obsolete stocks.

reviews.circular-and-bio-based-economies: The chapter began with recycling and ended far beyond it, with whole systems that keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value. The waste hierarchy and its R-hierarchy cousins rank the options: refusing and reducing at the top, then reuse, repair and remanufacturing, with recycling and energy recovery near the bottom. Industrial ecology, industrial symbiosis and material flow analysis treat factories like ecosystems, where one firm's waste becomes another's input. New business models sell light instead of lamps and share cars that sit idle 95% of the time, while the bioeconomy draws on renewable living resources. Yet physics and economics set limits: recovery can never be 100%, virgin plastic is often cheaper than recycled, and critics ask whether efficiency gains have ever cut total resource use.
